title: Data retention is mass surveillance of people’s phone and internet activity
text:
Skip to content

Close

Search

How would you best describe that thing you're looking for?

What is “data retention” for law enforcement?
It is the legal requirement for internet service providers to retain metadata about their users beyond what is necessary for the provision of the service (e.g. billing or network optimisation and security purposes) and to keep it solely so that it can later be accessed by law enforcement bodies and intelligence services.
What is metadata?
Metadata is data generated for the purpose of transmitting content in electronic communications services and networks. This includes mobile numbers of the sender and recipient, the time and duration of a call or an internet session, websites accessed, and the location of mobile devices. On a technical level, metadata is no longer needed once the transmission ends.
Metadata is very revealing about people’s private lives.

Systematic recording of location data will reveal a person’s permanent and temporary places of residence, political and religious preferences (e.g. participation in public demonstrations and religious ceremonies), health status (e.g. visit to a specialised clinic), sexual orientation (e.g. LGBT+ venues), or other sensitive aspects (e.g. visit to a lawyer’s office).
Metadata contains information about social or professional relations with other people (“social graph”).
Usage patterns for website visits and other internet services reveal an enormous amount of information about a person’s interest and state of mind.

Why is it important?

Metadata is more revealing than the content of communications, especially because metadata is highly structured, which makes it easy to analyse. Governments can easily profile and categorise entire populations solely based on metadata.
The Court of Justice of the EU rightly described metadata retention as creating a feeling of being under constant surveillance. This has a chilling effect on participation in public life, as individuals restrict their own civil liberties to avoid surveillance.
While data access requests may be specific and targeted, general and indiscriminate data retention treats everyone as a potential suspect. Surveillance without suspicion violates the presumption of innocence, which is an essential right in democratic societies.
Retention of vast amounts of personal data inevitably creates huge vulnerabilities to cyberattacks. Malicious actors can gain access to massive amounts of data and abuse it for identity theft or blackmail.
Data retention severely undermines the possibility of online anonymity. Anonymity is a question of safety for many, even a matter of life or death: investigative journalists, whistleblowers, crime survivors, political opponents, refugees, victims of transnational repression, artists, human rights defenders, and more. It supports the exercise of key fundamental rights such as freedom of expression and the freedom to receive and impart information.

Examples of harms caused by indiscriminate data retention

US telecom company AT&T was hacked by an attacker who stole the logs of calls and texts to more than 100 million customers over a six-month period in 2022.
In 2024 the Garda Síochána Ombudsman Commission (Ireland’s police watchdog) accessed journalists’ phone records to identify their sources as part of its own investigation into the Irish police, even though the journalists were not accused of any criminal offence.
In 2013, the Polish Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA) obtained access to billing data of a journalist who had reported on irregularities in the intelligence services. The CBA’s aim was to uncover their source’s identity. The journalist won the case in court, and the CBA published an official apology.

title: CVE-2026-115934 - SQL injection leading to privilege escalation
text:
9.8

CRITICAL
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-115934
SQL injection leading to privilege escalation

An unauthenticated SQL injection can occur on the front end of any site that uses craft.search to perform a search, allowing stacked query execution and enabling escalation to an administrator.

Note that this only affects MySQL/MariaDB.

Impact * SQL injection — The attribute parameter is concatenated into the query unsanitized, and because PDO runs with emulated prepares, stacked statements execute. This gives unauthenticated read and write access to the application database.
* Privilege escalation to administrator — The write primitive was used to set the admin flag on user ID 1 in the users table, confirmed by reading the value back. Craft short-circuits its permission checks on this single column, so no further changes were needed. The same primitive can overwrite any account’s password hash.

Update to the patched versions (4.18.9 and 5.11.2) to get the fix.

If you cannot update immediately, you can block front-end requests with %5Battribute%5D and [attribute] anywhere in the query string as a temporary mitigation.

title: CVE-2026-125120 - Mongoose: sanitizeFilter not applied on countDocuments
text:
9.8

CRITICAL
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-125120
Mongoose: sanitizeFilter not applied on countDocuments

Mongoose is a MongoDB object modeling tool designed to work in an asynchronous environment. Prior to 6.13.11, 7.8.12, 8.24.3, and 9.9.2, Mongoose countDocuments() does not apply the configured sanitizeFilter query selector injection defense. An application that enables sanitizeFilter and passes attacker-controlled filter values to countDocuments() can therefore process query operator objects as operators rather than literal values, causing the count to include documents that should not match and potentially undermining authorization or application logic based on that count. This issue is fixed in versions 6.13.11, 7.8.12, 8.24.3, and 9.9.2.

8.2

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-125117
Mongoose walks into inherited properties when hydrating, setting, and merging, allowing overwrites of built-in functions (denial of service) and shared schema state

Mongoose is a MongoDB object modeling tool designed to work in an asynchronous environment. Prior to 6.13.12, 7.8.13, 8.24.7, and 9.11.4, Mongoose can descend into inherited properties while loading database documents in init(), setting dotted paths in $__set, and merging update documents in utils.mergeClone. Attacker-controlled keys such as toString or valueOf can therefore cause Mongoose to write into shared built-in functions instead of an own property. A crafted document, Mixed path, non-strict document or subdocument, findOneAndReplace() replacement, chained update, or Query.prototype.merge() source can overwrite Object.prototype.toString.call, causing later queries on unrelated models to fail until the process restarts. Separately, when an attacker controls the dotted path passed to doc.set(path, value) for a subdocument configured with strict: false, descent through $__set can reach $__schema and alter shared validators or schema options for later documents. Mongoose already blocks __proto__, constructor, and prototype, so this issue overwrites properties on reachable shared objects rather than adding new properties directly to Object.prototype. This issue is fixed in versions 6.13.12, 7.8.13, 8.24.7, and 9.11.4.

AsyncSSH: SFTPServer Chroot Escape

AsyncSSH is a Python package which provides an asynchronous client and server implementation of the SSHv2 protocol on top of the Python asyncio framework. CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-123807
Signal K Server: Unauthenticated path traversal in resources-provider v2 API leads to JWT secret disclosure, admin impersonation and remote code execution

Signal K Server is a server application that runs on a central hub in a boat. From 2.0.0 until 2.34.0 for Signal K Server and from 1.0.0 until 1.5.3 for @signalk/resources-provider, the v2 REST route GET /signalk/v2/api/resources/:resourceType/:resourceId accepts an unsafe resourceId that can escape the intended resource directory. Deployments with allow_readonly enabled permit anonymous reads, while other deployments require a readonly user token. Reading security.json exposes the HS256 JWT signing secret and password hashes, allowing an attacker to forge an administrator token. Administrative access to POST /skServer/providers can then create an Execute provider that runs commands with the server process privileges and persists its configuration across restarts. This issue is fixed in Signal K Server 2.34.0 and @signalk/resources-provider 1.5.3.

title: Microsoft Fixes RCE Bug in Windows Paint After Weeks of Confusion
text: Alexander Culafi,Senior News Writer,Dark ReadingNovember 9, 20263 Min Read Microsoft recently patched a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Windows Paint, though details regarding how to fix the flaw seemingly remained unsettled for nearly a month.According to an advisory, the flaw, CVE-2026-83844, is an "out-of-bounds read in Windows Paint [that] allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code locally." It carries a high severity CVSS 3.1 score of 7.0.The advisory offers few technical details for defenders. Microsoft said acquiring RCE requires local access, meaning hands-on-keyboard or a direct remote connection to the attacker's machine. Some user interaction is also required; altogether, this may explain why the attack is "only" high severity rather than a 9 or 10 CVSS, as is so often associated with RCE flaws. Microsoft has observed no exploitation reports to date, further marking exploitation as "less likely."A Windows Paint patch is available now. The fixed version is 11.2609.401.0, and customers can see it under Paint > Settings > About. A Microsoft spokesperson tells Dark Reading, "A security update for Paint is available through the Microsoft Store, and customers with automatic Store updates enabled are already protected. We recommend customers check they are on the latest version and install the available updates to remain protected." Customers can also manually apply the update via Microsoft Store App > Downloads > Check for updates.A Curious Timeline for a Windows Paint CVE CVE-2026-83844 is an unusual vulnerability for multiple reasons, beyond it being a high-severity Paint vulnerability capable of RCE.As Brian Vitko, founder of device management software provider RFF, wrote in a blog post, Microsoft first disclosed the bug on Oct. 13, but there seemed to be no indication the reported fix (11.2605.91.0) was live, even as of Oct. 30. By Nov. 4, Vitko, the correct fixed version was listed in the security advisory (11.2609.401.0) but 11.2605.81.0 was the latest update available in the store. The correct version was added to the store on Nov. 6.The original version of the advisory FAQ, according to Vitko's post, said the attack could possibly be exploited, "by sending a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network."But the latest version of the FAQ reads, "For example, when the score indicates that the Attack Vector is Local and User Interaction is Required, this could describe an exploit in which an attacker, through social engineering, convinces a victim to download and open a specially crafted file from a website which leads to a local attack on their computer." Vitko tells Dark Reading that this latter explanation aligns more with his expectations for a vulnerability targeting Windows Paint, and that the wording may just be the result of standardized Microsoft FAQ language than speaking directly to the vulnerability."Paint isn't something that listens on the network. When it was published, it was CVSS 8.1 with a network attack vector, and the FAQ talked about 'a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network.' Microsoft changed that on Nov. 7: it's now 7.0, local, user interaction required, and the FAQ says an attacker 'convinces a victim to download and open a specially crafted file from a website,'" he says. "That makes a lot more sense for an image editor. Microsoft hasn't said anything more about the actual trigger."Dark Reading asked Microsoft for additional information regarding the update timeline. The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl. Linux systems that use both of these packages and meet certain other requirements can be hacked to give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts in a matter of seconds. *sshole became publicly known last Thursday and quickly stoked concerns it could lead to widespread compromise of Linux machines. Four days later, the prediction shows signs of becoming real.
Attackers conducting “mature intrusions”
Security firm Greynoise said Monday that honeypots it maintains in Southeast Asia have come under attack by a group it’s tracking as GT10. The group conducted “mature intrusions” into the systems, which Greynoise uses to detect attempted or successful attacks in real time. Greynoise subsequently gained access to a GT10 server that revealed potential other victims and some of the tools used in the campaign. A backdoor the group is using in the attacks contains Chinese language comments and appears to be generated with the use of AI.
Greynoise said that GT10 is also installing the Python3 release on machines that don’t already have it because the package is required to run the hacker’s backdoor, which is tracked under the name TAC Agent. TAC Agent supports a wide range of functions, including shell commands, system reconnaissance, and persistence. OpenSSH has released a fix that prevents attacks from working.

Researchers at security firm watchTowr said Friday that they, too, were seeing exploitation activity, which was related to botnets and cryptocurrency. Security firm Previdian has also reported similar activity. It said its company’s sensors have seen 20 exploitation attempts from 13 unique attacker IP addresses geolocated to nine countries.
The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123158, resides in OpenSSH, when it runs alongside musl, a Linux alternative to the widely used libc code library. Further, OpenSSH must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account access checks. Additionally, SSH configurations must (1) have at least one account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 function and (2) also be set to use passwordless accounts by way of specifying a “*” in the password field in the /etc/shadow file. Passwordless configurations are standard for certain types of accounts.
Exploits are triggered when an attacker enters passwords with more than 256 characters for a passwordless account. This step occurs when the OpenSSH server hashes the supplied password and checks it against the hash stored in /etc/shadow. The oversized password produces an error that causes musl’s password hashing function to return “*”. The attacks exploit the “misinterpretation of whether a string is intended to be a password hash,” Red Hat said.
Despite the multiple conditions necessary, CVE-2026-123158 poses a serious threat to a large base of machines, most notably those running Alpine, a lightweight distribution of Linux. The ease of exploitation allows hackers to direct malicious commands to any of the millions of SSH servers exposed to the Internet and identify potentially vulnerable ones in seconds. Anyone using OpenSSH should install the update promptly. Those using musl should investigate further.

title: C3RB3R attacks Synology NAS: how to protect your files | Kaspersky official blog
text:
Many people think of a home network-attached storage (NAS) device as a large hard drive connected to their router. They store videos, photos, documents, and backups on it, then barely think about the device for years. That’s a huge mistake.
In October 2026, attackers began infecting Synology NAS devices with C3RB3R (Cerber) ransomware. Many users report that they can no longer open files on their network storage, and that text files containing ransom demands are appearing in their folders. And this isn’t happening because someone accidentally downloaded a malicious file: anyone who forgot to update their network storage in time is at risk.
In this article, we explain exactly who’s at risk and how to protect your data.
Who C3RB3R targets and how the attack works
We’re used to thinking that malware gets onto a device after someone downloads a suspicious file or follows an attacker’s instructions. But the vast majority of C3RB3R infections happen without any user interaction at all — the attacker only needs to reach a vulnerable NAS service. Specialized scanners likely help find such devices by automatically looking for Synology NAS systems and checking their DiskStation Manager (DSM) version.
In October, many Synology owners began reporting C3RB3R attacks. Synology officially confirmed the issue and said the attackers were exploiting a vulnerability that had been fixed back in December 2024. Based on the description, this appears to be CVE-2024-10441 — a vulnerability that lets an attacker execute arbitrary code in the NAS operating system without authentication.
At the same time, researchers at 360.cn reported that the C3RB3R attacks they examined also involved two other critical vulnerabilities, each rated 9.8: CVE-2026-13639 and CVE-2026-13684. These vulnerabilities allow arbitrary file reads or writes and denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. Synology hasn’t confirmed that these vulnerabilities have been used in this campaign. The company patched them in its September DSM update.
Either way, the vulnerabilities mentioned above allow attackers to target a NAS remotely. For attackers to access your storage, get ransomware onto it, and run it, only two conditions need to be met:

You haven’t updated your network-attached storage for a long time
The Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) interface is accessible from the internet (or the local network)

That’s it. The attacker doesn’t need your password or any action from you. Every Synology NAS owner who hasn’t updated the system in time is at risk.
If you haven’t installed updates yourself recently and don’t remember whether automatic updates are enabled, we recommend first blocking internet access to your NAS and then updating the device manually as soon as possible — otherwise, you could easily end up among the victims.
Keep in mind that until the updates are installed, the device remains vulnerable to attacks from the local network. So, if your Synology NAS is accessible to other users on the LAN — for example, it’s shared with neighbors or connected to a university, office, or dorm network — the safest option is to disconnect the Ethernet cable and turn off Wi-Fi if your NAS model supports it. Then download the update files to your computer, disconnect the computer from both the wired network and Wi-Fi, connect the NAS directly to the computer with an Ethernet cable, and update its operating system and applications in a fully isolated environment.
Another strong reason to update your network storage is the recently discovered PHP vulnerabilities. Synology has already released urgent updates for its operating system and the Mail Station and Synology Calendar applications.
What happens to files after infection

ROV turned your validator into a forwarding policy source. The registries have strengthened their side of the RPKI, but the chain from repository to router runs on your infrastructure. When that chain breaks, it often breaks silently.

RPKI fails openRoute Origin Validation works. RPKI now covers about 70% of Internet routes, up from 54% a year earlier, and invalid announcements propagate poorly because enough of the network refuses to carry them.The Regional Internet Registries deserve much of the credit. Hosted RPKI made issuing ROAs take just a few clicks. The RIPE NCC and ARIN have brought ASPA online. And when something goes wrong, the RIRs publish post-mortems and make fixes. That openness is a big part of why operators trust RPKI enough to act on it.But acting on RPKI changes its role. Once your routers drop invalid routes, the VRP set they receive becomes forwarding policy. RPKI is designed to fail open: as RIPE NCC explained after its 2020 incidents, a revoked certificate or missing ROA leaves announcements as NotFound rather than Invalid, so they are not dropped. That protects reachability. It also means that when part of the chain breaks, routes can quietly move from Valid to NotFound - with no alert to tell you.The chainBetween a resource holder authorising an origin and your router acting on that authorisation are five links:CA account → Repository → Relying party → RTR session → Router policy

The RPKI trust chain. The registries operate the first two links. The last three run on your infrastructure.

A resource holder issues objects through a CA account. The RIR, or a delegated CA, publishes them in a repository. Your validator fetches and validates those objects, serves the results to your routers over RTR, and your routers apply them to the routes they receive.Every upstream failure reaches your network the same way: as a change in what your validator serves, meaning the validator is the place to watch.What has gone wrongThe examples below cover operational failures, a credential-based attack, and academic research. We are not aware of a publicly documented attack on the RTR protocol itself in the wild. The point is that every link has failed at least once, and yet the router rarely showed the failure.CA account: Orange EspañaOn 3 January 2024, Orange España, Spain's second-largest mobile operator, suffered a nationwide outage lasting several hours. A compromised password gave an attacker access to an RIR account with no two-factor authentication. The attacker signed ROAs directing about two million addresses to a non-Orange ASN. Networks enforcing ROV then dropped Orange's newly Invalid routes, exactly as designed.RIPE NCC's systems did what they were designed to do. Because the malicious changes were submitted through the legitimate interface, the account logs showed a successful login and an authorised action. The weak point was the account's credentials, not the registry. From the Internet's perspective, RPKI itself didn't fail. The signal was a large number of routes for one origin changing from Valid to Invalid within minutes.Repository: incidents at the RIRsThe RIRs have had their own incidents. What stands out is how they responded.In February 2020, a disk fault at RIPE NCC left objects stored but unpublished, with no alert raised. CVE-2026-124034, CVE-2026-124035: Issues with Amazon Braket SDK

Bulletin ID: 2026-175-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 11/09/2026 14:15 PM PST

Description:

Amazon Braket SDK is an open source Python library that customers use to run quantum tasks and hybrid jobs on Amazon Braket and retrieve their results, and it uses the Amazon Braket Schemas library to parse task results.

We identified CVE-2026-124034, an issue in the local hybrid job input data download in the Amazon Braket SDK. A remote authenticated user with S3 write access to a hybrid job's input data location might be able to overwrite arbitrary files, with the privileges of the user running the job, by supplying crafted S3 object keys.

We identified CVE-2026-124035, an issue in the error mitigation schema validation in Amazon Braket Schemas, the library the Amazon Braket SDK uses to parse quantum task results. A remote authenticated user with S3 write access to the quantum task output location might be able to execute arbitrary code on any machine that retrieves the quantum task results by supplying a crafted task result document. Please note, this is a follow-on fix to the prior advisory CVE-2026-9291.

Impacted versions:

CVE-2026-124034: amazon-braket-sdk >= 1.10.0 AND < 1.127.7
CVE-2026-124035: amazon-braket-schemas >= 1.17.0 AND < 1.32.2

Resolution:

CVE-2026-124034: This issue has been addressed in Amazon Braket SDK version 1.127.7. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.
CVE-2026-124035: This issue has been addressed in Amazon Braket Schemas version 1.32.2. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Workarounds:

Restrict S3 write access to the Braket task-output and local-job input data locations (and the job's IAM role) to trusted principals.

TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES

Queens Public Library, a New York City public library system serving approximately 2.3 million residents, was struck by a ransomware attack that encrypted its systems. The incident disrupted public computers, Wi-Fi, checkout equipment, digital media services, and its mobile application, while all 66 branches remained open.
Russian web hosting provider Beget sustained a destructive cyberattack on November 1 that wiped data across its cloud infrastructure and disrupted hundreds of websites. N-able takes N-central offline as alleged zero-day exploits surface

By Field Effect Security Intelligence Team

At a glance:

November 9: After public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities affecting N-central, N-able took hosted environments offline and advised those operating on-premises deployments to take their servers offline as well. Active exploitation not observed at time of advisory.

An individual or group operating under the name Oracle-Security released technical details and proof-of-concept (PoC) code for multiple alleged N-central vulnerabilities, including several exploit chains that reportedly lead to full server compromise.

The disclosures affect the management platform itself. If the reported exploit chains function as described, they could provide a path to the systems, credentials, and administrative functions already trusted by N-central.

Threat summary
On November 9, 2026, N-able announced it was responding to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities affecting N-central.
The company temporarily took hosted N-central environments offline and advised customers with on-premises deployments to do the same until further guidance is available. N-able said it had not observed active exploitation and is preparing a hotfix.
N-central is a Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) platform used to monitor systems, deploy software, execute scripts, manage patches, and perform administrative tasks across large numbers of endpoints from one console. Because it typically holds privileged access to managed infrastructure, a compromised N-central server can give attackers a path to downstream systems.
The disclosure originated from a GitHub account named Oracle-Security, which published a release titled "Able2Shell" in a repository labeled "0-Days/N-Central N-Able." It describes 33 alleged N-central vulnerabilities and includes technical writeups, screenshots, captured output, and Python PoC code. One file, anonymous_xxe_nable_rce.py, appears to demonstrate an unauthenticated XML External Entity (XXE) vulnerability that can be chained into Remote Code Execution (RCE).
The published material alleges a mix of authenticated and unauthenticated vulnerabilities across multiple components. According to the publisher’s PoCs and technical claims, the exploit chains could allow remote code execution, privilege escalation, administrator account creation, credential disclosure, configuration changes, account enumeration, audit record manipulation, remote-control session disruption, and device impersonation.

In July and August, threat actors exploited CVE-2026-18577, an authentication bypass vulnerability, to gain administrative access to vulnerable N-central deployments and pivot to managed systems through built-in remote management functionality.

An API key. Create one in Sekoia.io with permission to search events. Read-only is enough for searching; the massive export needs the SIC_MASSIVE_EXPORT_EVENTS permission.

Your region’s API host. The default is https://api.sekoia.io. Other regions have their own hosts, for example https://api.usa1.sekoia.io.

Query language. The API accepts the same queries as the Events page. The examples below use the classic “dork” syntax (term_lang: dork). Build and test the query in the UI first.

Export with the events search API

API="https://api.sekoia.io/v1"H="Authorization: Bearer $SEKOIA_API_KEY"# 1. create the search jobJOB=$(curl -sS -X POST "$API/sic/conf/events/search/jobs" -H "$H" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \  -d '{"term": "host.name:\"web-03\"", "earliest_time": "2026-10-19T00:00:00Z", "latest_time": "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z", "term_lang": "dork"}' \  | jq -r '.uuid')# 2. wait until the job is done (status 2)until [ "$(curl -sS -H "$H" "$API/sic/conf/events/search/jobs/$JOB" | jq -r '.status')" = "2" ]; do sleep 3; done# 3. read the events, 1,000 at a timeTOTAL=$(curl -sS -H "$H" "$API/sic/conf/events/search/jobs/$JOB" | jq '.total')for ((off=0; off<TOTAL; off+=1000)); do  curl -sS -H "$H" "$API/sic/conf/events/search/jobs/$JOB/events?limit=1000&offset=$off" | jq -c '.items[]'done > sekoia_web03_1019.jsonl

Events come back newest first. A job that fails never reaches status 2, so add a timeout if you script this for regular use.

For large exports, start the massive export on a finished job (POST /v1/sic/conf/events/search/jobs/<uuid>/export), wait for the task, then fetch the download link. The sekoia-event-exporter package on PyPI wraps this workflow.

Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file.

Sanitize.

Review.

When it goes wrong

SymptomLikely causeFixUI export stops at 500 eventsUI export limitUse the API, or the massive export401 or 403Key missing, or without search permissionCheck the key’s roleErrors from a valid keyWrong regional hostUse your region’s API hostThe wait loop never endsJob failed or was cancelledCheck the job status; narrow the queryOnly the newest eventsOffset paging not followedPage through with offset up to total

FAQ Dork or Sekoia Operating Language?Both exist. The API examples in Sekoia’s quickstart use dork; check which query languages your API key and endpoint accept.Can I export the events behind an alert?Yes: run an events search with filters for the alert, then export as above.

text:
En

LogTotal HOWTO

November 09, 2026
3 min read

Cloud SIEM runs on top of Datadog Log Management, so exporting “Cloud SIEM logs” means exporting the logs behind it. Use the Logs Search API, POST /api/v2/logs/events/search, with an API key and an application key, and follow the cursor until there’s no next page; each page holds up to 1,000 logs. For history beyond your index retention, read your log archives in S3, GCS or Azure Storage, or rehydrate them. Security signals are a separate API.

Datadog is where many cloud-native teams already keep their logs, which makes it the natural source for an investigation slice. Prime Core has 23,983 detection rules for Datadog, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get logs out, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

Two keys. The Logs Search API needs an API key (DD-API-KEY) and an application key (DD-APPLICATION-KEY). The application key must belong to a user, or a service account, that can read the logs, and if it’s scoped, it needs log read access.

Your Datadog site. The API host follows your site: api.datadoghq.com (US1), api.us3.datadoghq.com, api.us5.datadoghq.com, api.datadoghq.eu, api.ap1.datadoghq.com and others. Use the one matching your login URL.

Retention. Indexed logs are searchable for as long as their index keeps them. Older logs exist only in archives, if you set any up.

Export with the Logs Search API

DD="https://api.datadoghq.eu"BODY='{"filter": {"query": "host:web-03 source:sshd", "from": "2026-10-19T00:00:00Z", "to": "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"}, "page": {"limit": 1000}, "sort": "timestamp"}': > dd_web03_1019.jsonlCURSOR=""while :; do  REQ=$(echo "$BODY" | jq --arg c "$CURSOR" 'if $c != "" then .page.cursor = $c else . end')  RESP=$(curl -sS -X POST "$DD/api/v2/logs/events/search" \    -H "DD-API-KEY: $DD_API_KEY" -H "DD-APPLICATION-KEY: $DD_APP_KEY" \    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "$REQ")  echo "$RESP" | jq -c '.data[]' >> dd_web03_1019.jsonl  CURSOR=$(echo "$RESP" | jq -r '.meta.page.after // empty')  [ -z "$CURSOR" ] && breakdone# raw messages onlyjq -r '.attributes.message' dd_web03_1019.jsonl > dd_web03_1019.log

The API is rate limited. For big windows, expect it to take a while, and back off when you see 429.

Older logs: archives

If you configured log archives, Datadog writes compressed JSON files to your bucket, organized by date and hour. Download the hours you need and decompress them:

aws s3 cp s3://my-dd-archive/dt=20261019/ ./dd-archive/ --recursivezcat ./dd-archive/*/*.json.gz > dd_archive_1019.jsonl

Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file.]

When it goes wrong

SymptomLikely causeFix403 ForbiddenApplication key lacks log read accessUse a key from a user or service account that can read logsValid keys, no dataWrong Datadog siteUse your site’s API hostNothing older than a few daysIndex retentionRead the archives, or rehydrate429 Too Many RequestsRate limitWait, then continue with the same cursorOnly 1,000 resultsCursor not followedLoop until meta.page.after is empty

title: How to Export SentinelOne Logs
text:
En

LogTotal HOWTO

November 09, 2026
3 min read

SentinelOne keeps three kinds of data worth exporting: endpoint telemetry, threats, and activities (the audit trail of what users and agents did in the console). Telemetry lives in Singularity Data Lake and has its own guide. Threats and activities come out of the management API (https://<console>.sentinelone.net/web/api/v2.1) with an ApiToken header, as JSON, page by page with a cursor.

When something goes wrong on a SentinelOne-protected network, the activity log often answers the uncomfortable questions. Who disabled that agent? Who added that exclusion? Who marked the threat as benign? Prime Core has 14,741 detection rules for SentinelOne, mapped to 644 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get the data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

An API token. Create a service user (or use your own user) with view rights at the account or site that holds the data, and generate its API token. Tokens expire; note when.

Your console URL. It’s the hostname you log in to, for example https://usea1-example.sentinelone.net.

Export activities and threats

S1="https://usea1-example.sentinelone.net/web/api/v2.1"H="Authorization: ApiToken $S1_API_TOKEN"URL="$S1/activities?createdAt__gte=2026-10-19T00:00:00Z&createdAt__lt=2026-10-20T00:00:00Z&limit=1000": > s1_activities_1019.jsonlNEXT=""while :; do  RESP=$(curl -sS -H "$H" "${URL}${NEXT:+&cursor=$NEXT}")  echo "$RESP" | jq -c '.data[]' >> s1_activities_1019.jsonl  NEXT=$(echo "$RESP" | jq -r '.pagination.nextCursor // empty')  [ -z "$NEXT" ] && breakdone

For threats, swap /activities for /threats and save to another file. Both endpoints accept more filters, such as site IDs or activity types.

What to look for in activities

Look for agents being uninstalled, disabled or put into a less protective mode. Watch for new exclusions, especially broad paths. Check threats that were marked as resolved or benign without investigation, and policy changes. Look closely at console logins from unfamiliar places. Any of these, right before or during an incident, is worth a second look.

Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file.

Sanitize.

Review.

When it goes wrong

SymptomLikely causeFix401Token expired, or the header isn’t ApiToken <token>Generate a new token; check the headerEmpty results with a valid tokenToken’s scope doesn’t cover the siteUse a user at the right scopeOnly 1,000 recordsCursor not followedLoop on pagination.nextCursorNo process telemetry hereTelemetry isn’t in the management API

FAQ Can I get the agent’s own logs?The console can fetch agent logs from an endpoint for troubleshooting. Those are diagnostic files for support, not security telemetry.What about Deep Visibility?Deep Visibility was the earlier telemetry search. Current consoles use Singularity Data Lake; see that guide.

title: How to Export Carbon Black Logs
text:
En

LogTotal HOWTO

November 09, 2026
3 min read

For a targeted pull from Carbon Black Cloud, use the Platform Search API. Create a process search job, wait until all backends have answered, and fetch the results as JSON. For bulk, continuous export, set up the Data Forwarder, which writes endpoint events, alerts and watchlist hits to your own S3 bucket as compressed JSON. Carbon Black EDR, the on-premises product formerly called Response, has a different API.

Carbon Black, now part of Broadcom, records process activity on a lot of corporate endpoints. Prime Core has 15,590 detection rules for Carbon Black, mapped to 638 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get the data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

An API key and your org key. Create an API key whose access level allows process search, and note the API ID and secret. The org key is shown in the console’s API access settings. Together they make the header X-Auth-Token: <secret>/<id>.

Your environment’s host. Carbon Black Cloud runs several environments, each with its own hostname (for example defense.conferdeploy.net or defense-eu.conferdeploy.net). Use the one in your console URL.

Retention. Process data is kept for a limited time, depending on your subscription. The Data Forwarder is how you keep more.

Option 1: Process search API

CBC="https://defense.conferdeploy.net"ORG="<org_key>"H="X-Auth-Token: $CB_API_SECRET/$CB_API_ID"# 1. start the search jobJOB=$(curl -sS -X POST "$CBC/api/investigate/v2/orgs/$ORG/processes/search_jobs" \  -H "$H" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \  -d '{"query": "device_name:ws-042", "time_range": {"start": "2026-10-19T00:00:00Z", "end": "2026-10-20T00:00:00Z"}, "fields": ["*"], "rows": 10000}' \  | jq -r '.job_id')# 2. wait until every backend has answereduntil curl -sS -H "$H" "$CBC/api/investigate/v2/orgs/$ORG/processes/search_jobs/$JOB/results?rows=0" \      | jq -e '.contacted == .completed' >/dev/null; do sleep 3; done# 3. fetch the resultscurl -sS -H "$H" "$CBC/api/investigate/v2/orgs/$ORG/processes/search_jobs/$JOB/results?start=0&rows=10000" \  | jq -c '.results[]' > cb_ws042_1019.jsonl

This returns process records. Network connections, file and registry modifications for a process are available through the process event details APIs. The official Python SDK (carbon-black-cloud-sdk) wraps all of this.

Option 2: Data Forwarder (bulk)

In the console, configure a Data Forwarder to an S3 bucket you own and choose the data types: endpoint events, alerts, watchlist hits. Files arrive as compressed JSON, one record per line. For an investigation, download the time range and filter by device:

aws s3 cp s3://my-cb-forwarder/<prefix>/ ./cb-fwd/ --recursivezcat ./cb-fwd/**/*.gz | jq -c 'select(.device_name == "ws-042")' > cb_fwd_ws042.jsonl

Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file.

Sanitize.

Review.

When it goes wrong

SymptomLikely causeFix401Header in the wrong order, or a bad keyX-Auth-Token: <secret>/<id>403Access level lacks process searchUse a custom access level with search rightsResults look incompleteFetched before contacted == completedWait for the job to finishConnection errorsWrong environment hostnameUse the host from your console URLNothing older than a few weeksRetentionUse Data Forwarder files

FAQ Which product do I have?If you log in to a cloud console, it’s Carbon Black Cloud. If you run your own server, it’s Carbon Black EDR, which has a different API.Can I export alerts too?Yes, through the alerts API or the Data Forwarder. For LogTotal, the endpoint events are the main input.

Police say about 10,000 phones a day lost service; most victims were tourists.Japan has had no 2G network for over a decade. Phones still accept it. text:
Key takeaways

On November 7, Japan's telecom regulator and the Tokyo Metropolitan Police caught a man running a fake mobile base station from a car in Ginza, Tokyo's luxury shopping district. Police say it is the first case in Japan of obstructing mobile communications this way.
The device jammed nearby phones' 4G and 5G service, pulled them onto its own 2G signal, and sent Chinese-language SMS claiming the recipient's card payments had been suspended, with a link to a site asking for card details.
According to Jiji Press, the police believe about 10,000 phones a day were knocked out of service within at least 500 meters, and that the same thing happened in Shinjuku and Shibuya. Eighteen people, mainly Chinese tourists, have reported losses of about ¥4 million since January 2025.
Japan has had no 2G network for over a decade. The attack works because phones still accept a 2G connection, and 2G does not let the phone check that the base station is genuine.
Users can protect themselves by turning off 2G where their phone allows it, and by treating SMS that arrive just after a sudden loss of signal with suspicion.

What happened#
According to the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications' Kanto Bureau of Telecommunications, it carried out a joint enforcement operation with the Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department in Chuo City, Tokyo, on November 7, against an illegal radio station set up in a vehicle. It has filed a criminal complaint against one person under the Radio Act, for opening an unlicensed radio station, a fake base station, and for obstructing radio communications used for telecommunications services.
Jiji Press reported that the man, a Chinese national, was arrested on the spot in Ginza, and that the police have also sent the case to prosecutors for obstructing important radio communications, those of NTT Docomo. According to Jiji, it is the first case in Japan of this kind of obstruction of mobile phone service. The man denies the charges. The police are investigating whether others were involved.
The problem was not new. In May 2025, the ministry warned that equipment suspected to be illegal radio stations, "so-called fake base stations", was causing interference in some cities including around Tokyo, knocking phones out of service and sending phishing SMS. NTT Docomo issued the same warning and said it was helping the ministry.
How the attack works#
A fake base station, often called an SMS blaster, pretends to be a mobile operator's cell tower:

It transmits on the same frequencies as the real network, strongly enough to jam phones' 4G and 5G connections nearby. The phone shows no signal.
The phone then looks for any network it can use, and finds the fake station's 2G signal.
In 2G, the phone authenticates itself to the network, but the network does not authenticate itself to the phone. The phone cannot tell that the "tower" is fake.
The fake station sends SMS directly to every phone that connected, without going through any operator, and so without any operator's spam filtering.

In this case, according to Jiji, the messages were in Chinese and said the recipient's card payments had been suspended because of possible fraud abroad. They led to a site that asked for card details.
Why tourists, and why Ginza#
The places named, Ginza, Shinjuku and Shibuya, are where foreign visitors shop. Most of the people who reported losses were Chinese tourists. A message in Chinese, about card payments, arriving in a shopping district, fits that audience. A tourist who has just used a card abroad is also more likely to believe that a bank has flagged a payment.
Japan has no 2G network#
Japan's mobile operators shut down their last 2G services more than a decade ago, and the GSM standard used by these devices was never used in Japan at all. That does not protect phones here: most smartphones still support 2G for roaming, and will connect to a 2G signal if nothing else is available. Jiji Press quotes a university expert as […]

Republican committee leaders sent a letter to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang asking him to brief them about his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang in a closed-door session on Nov. 18. (Image: Shutterstock)

House lawmakers are demanding answers from Nvidia about how the advanced semiconductor maker prevents foreign intelligence services from targeting its executives and technology after reports linked CEO Jensen Huang to a suspected Chinese spy.See Also: Frictionless Security: How AI is Redefining Access in Highly Regulated Industries
The Republican chairs of the House intelligence, foreign affairs and China committees sent a letter to Huang asking him to brief them in a closed-door session on Nov. 18. The lawmakers want to know how Nvidia protects itself from foreign espionage and what contact Huang has had with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive, describing her as a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia's board has opened its own independent investigation.
Rep. Rick Crawford, R-Ark., who chairs the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, signed the letter with House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla., and House Select Committee on China Chair John Moolenaar, R-Mich. They wrote that Congress must determine "the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk," calling Chinese infiltration of advanced U.S. technology central to their committees' investigations.
Nvidia's board, which said Sunday that it "has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised," has put independent directors and outside counsel in charge of its own review.
Huang apologized to employees in a Sunday memo, writing, "I was unfaithful to my wife." The memo, which voiced support for the board's probe, made no mention of Alice Huang.
Megaspeed is a Nvidia customer and sells artificial intelligence computing services out of Singapore. Alice Huang is not related to the Nvidia CEO.
Singapore police have said they are still investigating Megaspeed over suspected violations of local law, while the city-state's Ministry of Home Affairs said Oct. 31 that its officials never flagged Alice Huang's dealings with Jensen Huang as a concern and had not investigated her ties to China.
In April, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy warned that foreign actors were using jailbreaks and networks of proxy accounts to extract capabilities from U.S. frontier AI models (see: White House Warns of AI Model 'Extraction' Campaigns).
David Reber, Nvidia's chief security officer, argued in an August 2025 blog post that hidden hardware controls such as kill switches "would be a gift to hackers and hostile actors." The post went up days after the Cyberspace Administration of China called in Nvidia over alleged security risks in its H20 chip, as some U.S. lawmakers pushed for location verification on export-controlled processors (see: Nvidia Pushes Back on Chinese 'Kill-Switch' Claims).
Huang has argued that U.S. export bans give Chinese chipmakers an edge. The Trump administration reversed restrictions on Nvidia's H20 sales to China in 2025 and later approved sales of the more powerful H200. Huang traveled with President Donald Trump to Beijing in May (see: Go-Ahead for AI Chip Sales to 10 Chinese Firms Raise Alarms).
Democrats, who won control of both chambers in last week's midterm elections, take over committee gavels when the new Congress convenes in January.

Technical Analysis
The vulnerability is classified as CWE-306 — Missing Authentication for Critical Function. Per the NVD description, IBM Guardium Data Protection 12.2 is vulnerable to an authentication bypass that allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass IP-based access controls and access the Guardium management interface.
Breaking this into its component security properties:

Authentication bypass (the core defect). A critical function (the management interface) does not adequately enforce authentication before granting access. CWE-306 captures the class where a resource that requires an authenticated principal is reachable without one. Because the flaw is pre-authentication, no credentials, session tokens, or MFA factors are needed; exploitability is therefore conditional only on network reachability of the endpoint.

IP-based access control bypass (a secondary control failure). Guardium deployments commonly restrict administrative access to trusted management subnets or allow-listed source IPs. The description states the bypass permits crossing this boundary. This means defense-in-depth relying solely on network placement (management VLAN segmentation, firewall allow-lists, VPN restriction) is explicitly defeated by the flaw — a control that administrators frequently treat as their primary compensating safeguard.

Remote, low-complexity exploitation. The CVSS vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N indicates exploitation: over the network, with no attack complexity beyond sending crafted requests, no privileges, and no user interaction. S:U (Scope Unchanged) means the exploited component and impacted component remain the same security authority; C:H/I:H/A:H reflect total loss of confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the management interface's data and operations.

Attack surface. The Guardium management interface — the administrative web console and its underlying HTTP(S) services consumed by administrators — is the exposure point. Guardium management nodes are frequently deployed with web UI reachability from internal networks and, in misconfigured or externally exposed cases, from the internet. Image: Shutterstock
The defining weakness of American security isn't that we get attacked. It's that we often can't establish what's been done to us. The threats that matter most behave like black ice on a highway. They aren't so much hidden as indistinguishable from the road, and you find out the difference only after things are spinning out of control.See Also: Your Face Is Your Boarding Pass: How Biometric Identity Is Redefining the Way We Travel
I kept reaching the same conclusion as I wrote my latest book, "The Invisible War: Cybercrime, Nation-State Competition and the Rise of AI Agents." It traces a quarter century of attacks on American networks and infrastructure, from incidents at a nuclear plant to artificial intelligence agents running espionage campaigns largely on their own.
The book - which Wiley will publish in September 2027 - matches what I learned as an intelligence officer long before I started writing about any of this.
This week, the stunning dislosure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive U.S. intelligence suspects was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, is a great example of the black ice ahead for the United States and the AI industry.
So far, the media coverage is missing the mark. It isn't wrong. It is pointed at the wrong things.
Some of my colleagues in the trade media immediately reduced the story to a fairly conventional discussion about AI supply-chain risk and vendor compliance. Bloomberg estimated that the premarket slide would erase roughly $225 billion in market value, though that was an early-trading snapshot rather than a closing result; Yahoo Finance and IBTimes UK reported share declines of 4% to 4.5%. Fortune catalogued the CEO's changing statements: In October he had called his dealings with Alice Huang "completely normal and not unusual." The Spectator argued that China is "the real loser" because its "ham-fisted" operation backfired. Beijing's Global Times asked whether the scrutiny was a "political witch hunt."
Supply chain due diligence, CEO succession, valuation, a spy-novel plot and a propaganda counterpunch are all legitimate stories. None of them gets to the sentence that matters most, which comes from Nvidia's board, which says it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised."
I spent enough time around damage assessments to know what "no reason to believe" usually means. It means nobody has an instrument capable of producing a reason. A board investigation run by independent directors and outside counsel can examine emails and expense reports. It can't tell you where tens of thousands of GPUs ended up, and it can't tell you whether a CEO's views on export policy were nudged by someone whose job, if U.S. intelligence is right, was to nudge them. As Tech Times noted on Nov. 9, the probe "does not, on its face, address where Nvidia compute ends up, so clearing Huang would leave the chip-visibility question open."
Start with the hardware. "Compute" is the processing power, mostly from Nvidia's graphics processors, used to train and run AI models. Export controls are the Commerce Department's rules on which of those chips can be sold to whom. They exist because compute is no longer just a commercial input. It's the industrial base for AI-enabled military and intelligence operations, the modern equivalent of shell casings and powder.

Cyber Exam Prep Should Not Take a Third of Your Year
AI Automates Cyber Compliance Tasks, Cutting Exam Prep Time for Lean Security Teams

Randy Lindberg

Image: Rivial Data Security
Most security teams at credit unions and community banks consist of one to three members. I have worked with hundreds of them over the past 25 years, and the pattern holds at a $300 million credit union and at a $5 billion bank. The people are good. The math is not.See Also: Your Face Is Your Boarding Pass: How Biometric Identity Is Redefining the Way We Travel

Here's the math. A typical program carries about 200 controls across 40 systems. That is 8,000 control instances, each one needing an owner, evidence and a review date. Practitioners tell us audit and exam prep takes up to a third of the year. That time comes straight out of the work that actually reduces risk.

The Tools Have Not Fixed It

Most cyber governance, risk and compliance software track the work. Security teams enter the controls, upload the evidence, map it to the framework and build the examiner package by hand. The software is a filing cabinet with a dashboard on the front.

Newer products have added artificial intelligence features, and most of them do the same thing: read what you already wrote and suggest a paragraph. That is assistance. It saves a few minutes but leaves the work right where it was.

Here's the question I would ask any vendor this year. When the AI has completed its task, is the work done, or is it my turn?

What 'Done' Looks Like

On Nov. 10, Rivial Data Security is launching Rivial.ai, a software that performs the cyber GRC compliance task for lean security teams in regulated industries.

Drop in any document and Rivial.ai recognizes it as evidence, links it to the control, system and obligation it satisfies, and updates each record. It evaluates whether the document supports the control and flags the risk when it does not. Drop in an examiner's request list and a package comes back in minutes: a folder and a narrative for every item, plus one response file ready for the portal.

That's the difference between a tool that holds your compliance program and one that runs it.

Nothing Goes Final Without a Person

I want to be direct about this, because it is the part regulated institutions should care about most. Every change Rivial.ai makes is a recommendation your team accepts or rejects. Every action is logged. Rivial Data Security's own experts review what the AI produces. When the examiner arrives, they get organized evidence and a trail showing where each file came from and who approved it.

AI that nobody can explain doesn't belong in front of a National Credit Union Administration or Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation examiner. AI with a named reviewer and an audit trail does.

Where the Time Goes Instead

When the compliance work is handled, the job changes. The hours that used to go to chasing evidence and assembling binders go toward tasks that actually matter: minimizing the risk the assessment found, getting controls to hold on every system instead of most of them and walking into the exam with fewer findings than last year.

You're familiar with how examinations are conducted today. The program stalls for a quarter while everyone proves what was done instead of doing more of it. A team that stays exam-ready all year doesn't stall. The CISO who runs that kind of program stops being the person buried in the document request and becomes the one leadership trusts to say where the institution stands and what comes next. That's the seat this work is supposed to earn you, and it's difficult to earn when one-third of your year goes to building binders.

If you want to see what an examiner package looks like when the AI builds it, and a person signs off, explore Rivial.ai.

title: CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents
text:
A press release from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) today:
Today, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) unveiled the updated cyber incident reporting form, an enhanced web-enabled questionnaire available on CISA’s Incident Reporting Portal for reporting cyber incidents. By improving data quality, the more robust form strengthens the effectiveness and efficiency of national cyber defense. For instance, the new form will help CISA correlate related cyber threat activity to identify a larger trend from what otherwise would appear as independent incidents.
The new cyber incident reporting form is guided by community feedback CISA has received over the years and the agency’s efforts to improve data quality that enables rapid yet thorough threat analysis. For example, questions about the type of incident are more comprehensive and seek more granular information, including whether the incident involved malware, social engineering, hacking techniques or an insider threat. Also, questions about observed activity now incorporate the MITRE ATT&CK® Framework, language about adversary behavior that is familiar to the cyber community.
“In the team sport of cybersecurity, one organization’s detection is another’s protection,” said Acting Executive Assistant Director for Cybersecurity Chris Butera. “As the national coordinator for critical infrastructure cybersecurity and resilience, CISA is able to leverage such incident reporting to identify emerging cyber campaigns, warn potential targets, and strengthen the Nation’s collective defense.”
While only federal civilian agencies are required to report, CISA encourages any organization that experiences a cyber incident to voluntarily report.
For more information, please visit the Frequently Asked Questions webpage.

SEGA disclosure and the data involved
Japanese gaming company SEGA reported that the incident exposed 2.2 million newsletter subscriber email addresses and also “92,300 records with additional information yet to be determined.” The affected distribution covered 11 newsletters linked to SEGA and SEGA Fave products and services. SEGA said the compromised dataset did not include customer names, dates of birth, gender, addresses, phone numbers, credit card details, or account passwords.

The company said a web server vulnerability and problems in its system environment contributed to the incident, but that the exact intrusion method and timing remain under investigation.
The timeline of ARARA's disclosures shows a rapid expansion of the known impact. ARARA had earlier estimated a smaller scope and on October 29 assured SEGA that no data compromise had occurred. After uncovering the fuller extent of the incident, ARARA notified SEGA on November 3 and shared detailed information with the gaming company between November 5 and 8.
ARARA also reported that attackers abused their access to the service to send over 7 million emails impersonating credit card companies in late October.

title: Cyber-attack on French supermarket freezers has geopolitical context
text: Empty refrigerators at an Intermarche supermarket in Paris the day after the cyberattack. In the same year, hackers affiliated with Iran displayed the slogan “down with Israel” on the screens of water-control equipment made by an Israeli firm.Now France has attributed an attack on supermarket fridges to hackers operating under the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a key branch of Iran’s military establishment.There was no message this time, but the disruption made headlines around the world. Some refrigerators had their temperature turned up so high they caught fire. ‌In the hours after the hack, supermarket employees dumped piles of perished meat and melted ice-cream into rubbish containers.France’s foreign minister described it as an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” and promised “Europe-wide sanctions” would be imposed against those responsible.View image in fullscreenAn employee fills boxes of perished goods outside an Intermarche supermarket in Paris the day after the cyber-attack. Those attacks have not been officially attributed to Iran, but the French announcement is the first to implicate the state in this type of hack.skip past newsletter promotion after newsletter promotionWho is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why? Read moreRafe Pilling, a senior director at Sophos, a cybersecurity firm, said the relatively unsophisticated nature of the attack – hackers used default passwords to access fridge controls – was in line with Iranian capabilities. “The attacks themselves were not particularly complex,” he said.Pilling said there was now a presumption the French attacks and a wave of rogue defrosting hacks across Europe last week were linked.Hostile cyber operations against the west tend to come from a vexatious quartet of China, Russia, Iran and North Korea. All have different aims and characteristics: China has focused on industrial espionage and mass data gathering, Russia on disrupting enemy infrastructure and spreading disinformation, and North Korea on hacking crypto exchanges because it needs money. Iran, according to Pilling, wants to put a shot across the bow of its enemies.View image in fullscreenBoxes of perished goods outside an Intermarche supermarket in Paris the day after the cyber-attack. Photograph: Lucien Libert/ReutersHot fridges, a fake nuclear alert and a $6bn heist: are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic?Read more“In general Iran uses cyber-attacks to project power internationally and to signal their political displeasure with regional and international adversaries,” Pilling said.The fridge hacks came as the UK’s national cybersecurity centre warned the country is in the “foothills” of a new level of cyber threat – and should expect a “huge rise” in the volume of incidents. title: The Guardian view on the British Library: don’t privatise the reading rooms | Editorial
text: The British Library. ‘As a national institution, it is a place in which everyone has a stake.’ Photograph: Old Town Tourist/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe British Library. ‘As a national institution, it is a place in which everyone has a stake.’ Photograph: Old Town Tourist/Alamy The Guardian view on the British Library: don’t privatise the reading roomsEditorialCybercriminals are to blame for the current crisis. But renting out study space will not lead to recovery It holds two copies of Magna Carta, the charter that set limits on royal power in 1215. It has the sole surviving manuscript of the Anglo-Saxon epic Beowulf and notebooks by some of the most beloved authors in the English language: Jane Austen, William Blake, Virginia Woolf. Also in the British Library’s red-brick London building is the original, illustrated version of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland – given as an early Christmas gift to Alice Liddell in 1864. On handwritten drafts of Wilfred Owen’s tragic poem Dulce et Decorum est, visitors can see suggestions made by his friend Siegfried Sassoon.But neither display cases filled with treasures such as these nor vast digital archives, basement storage rooms, six cafes and a shop have been sufficient to arm the library against a sea of troubles that first threatened it three years ago, when hackers raided its computers for personal data and demanded a £600,000 ransom. Its long-serving chief executive, Roly Keating, took the decision to step down once the worst of the cyber-attack – one of the most serious in the UK’s history – had been dealt with. His replacement, Rebecca Lawrence, lasted less than a year before resigning in the middle of a strike over pay. Now, a new row has broken out over plans to rent out three of the library’s reading rooms and outsource security.The British Library is, of course, not alone in seeking novel ways to generate revenue from its open-access public building. Private and corporate private views are routine at blockbuster exhibitions; the early weeks of the British Museum’s Bayeux tapestry show were marred by a row about an ill-judged invitation to Peter Thiel, the tech billionaire. But reading rooms are unlike temporary exhibitions in that they are permanent. These are spaces designed for people to read and study in. Handing three of them over to a private contractor to operate commercially, as the British Library proposes, would change the character of a cherished institution.View image in fullscreenDr Paul Bate. Photograph: British LibraryIts new boss, Dr Paul Bate, has been in post for less than a week. He urgently needs to grip the situation and give a fuller account to staff, users and the public of what is going on. As an arm’s-length body, the library is overseen by a board. But since 84% of its £170m annual budget comes from the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, ministers too should be constructively engaged.It is widely accepted that the damage to finances and morale caused by the hackers, following the Covid pandemic, lies behind the current woes. A report this summer from the public accounts committee of MPs blamed the government for the lack of a strategic approach to cybersecurity. Politicians must take responsibility for past mistakes and help England’s national library to avoid a protracted crisis.As trade unions have pointed out, outsourcing the library’s security staff would be contrary to the government’s commitment to insourcing. Privatising sections would undermine a valued public space that is both open to all, and an essential component of a neglected higher‑education ecosystem. The British Library – formerly part of the British Museum – was established more than 50 years ago; the St Pancras building is approaching its 30th anniversary. As a national institution, it is a place in which everyone has a stake. Passwords and API keys that developers typed into commands they approved in Claude Code are sitting in public GitHub repositories, where anyone can read them.

When a user selects "Yes, and don't ask again," Anthropic's AI coding assistant can save the command, word-for-word, including the secret, in a project settings file.

Software security company Apiiro said yesterday that 1,122 public copies of that file hold at least one secret, though it did not test whether any still work. One company the researchers notified earlier this week confirmed its key had been live.

The file is .claude/settings.local.json. Removing it from a project does not undo the leak, because older versions stay in git history and in forks of the repository. The researchers' advice is to rotate first: change every password, token, and key the file has ever held, then clean up.

How a Secret Lands in the File

By default, Claude Code asks before it runs most shell commands. If the user picks "Yes, and don't ask again," it saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json inside the project, according to its permissions documentation. Matching commands then run without asking in later sessions.

The rule covers only what the prompt offered. Sometimes that is a pattern, such as npm test *, and sometimes one exact command. When it is the exact command, any password or token typed into it is saved too, in plain text.

In public files, the researchers found saved commands with the secret still inside, and they reproduced the behavior with the latest models, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1.

Claude Code tries to keep the file out of git. The first time it writes the file in a git repository, it adds the file to the user's global git excludes, its settings documentation says. Git on that computer then ignores the file in every repository.

That protection stays in one user's git settings on one computer. It does nothing for a file that was already committed, the researchers say. Claude Code never adds the file to the project's own .gitignore, so the protection does not travel with the project.

In 539 of the 1,105 repositories the researchers traced, a commit listing Claude as a co-author changed the file. They take this to mean Claude often commits the file itself.

What Apiiro Found

Apiiro's search of public GitHub found 104,185 copies of the file in 103,617 repositories, its research write-up shows. About 1.1% of them, or 1,122 copies, hold at least one secret. Together they hold 1,379 different secrets.

A value counted as a secret when it matched a known key format, or when a password or token sat beside the address of a public server. An AI reviewer also had to agree. The researchers do not say whether anyone has used these secrets.

More than a third of the secrets open a database directly, including 379 database passwords. Others include 43 SSH logins for public servers, 42 tokens for GitHub, GitLab and npm, and 23 AWS keys.

Among the owners of these files are 63 organizations, mostly software companies of all sizes. The strongest cases include a database vendor's own admin-level cloud key and the owner password of a medical-records database, the researchers say.

As of Monday, every file with a secret was still on its repository's default branch, and in half of those repositories it had been there for at least 217 days.

Older versions of the file contain 734 more secrets across 509 repositories that are not present in any current copy, usually because the file was deleted. Forks spread the files further: 211 forks of 74 repositories carry the same secrets as the originals.

An attacker broke into AWS accounts belonging to multiple Qubole customers between October 14 and October 26 and stole stored secrets and data, cloud security company Wiz said today.

The attacker used credentials for an AWS account that Qubole's platform uses to reach those customers. How the attacker got those credentials has not been disclosed.

Qubole, a data lake platform owned by Idera, operates within its customers' AWS accounts. To let it in, a customer creates an IAM role, which is an AWS identity with its own set of permissions.

The role's trust policy allows Qubole's AWS account to assume the role, granting those permissions. Each request to do this, called AssumeRole, must include a matching code from Qubole known as an External ID.

Apart from the attack, most of the roles the attacker assumed were unused, according to Wiz's researchers. But each role still trusted Qubole's account, so the attacker's requests worked.

Any organization that has connected Qubole to AWS, even one that no longer uses it, should check its CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward. The sign to look for is an AssumeRole request from the account Qubole's platform uses, 805246085872, that came from an address outside AWS.

The researchers did not say whether the credentials have since been disabled or whether the activity has stopped. Neither Qubole nor Idera had posted a statement about the attack on their websites when The Hacker News checked today.

Why the Roles Let the Attacker In

Every AssumeRole request tied to the attacker carried an External ID and was accepted, the researchers said in their technical analysis.

AWS accepts an AssumeRole request for such a role when it comes from the trusted account and includes the correct External ID. The code is not treated as a secret, and anyone with access to the role can view it, according to AWS's external ID guidance.

Sentra spotted the activity in several of its customers' environments and alerted the researchers.

In the accounts the researchers examined, the attacker looked for stored credentials. It read environment variables for Lambda functions, pulled secrets from Secrets Manager, and read values from the SSM Parameter Store.

It then ran the credentials it had found through TruffleHog to test whether they worked. These were the victims' own AWS access keys, Entra ID client secrets, and Okta client credentials.

The attacker also copied data out of S3. It retrieved data from any bucket a role could access rather than searching for specific data, and sometimes downloaded an entire bucket in a single session.

The researchers have not linked this campaign to any other publicly reported activity, and say the targeting does not match what state-backed groups usually go after.

Qubole also lets customers connect with AWS access keys instead of a role. From October 8 to October 11, an attacker used customers' own AWS access keys, which the researchers believe had been set up for Qubole.

That attacker then compromised a few of the victims' cloud environments. This activity has not been linked to the AssumeRole abuse.

How to Check Your Accounts

Wiz's hunting guidance covers CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward in every AWS account that holds a Qubole role. Look for:

Account: AssumeRole requests where userIdentity.accountId is 805246085872 and sourceIPAddress is not an AWS address. The researchers saw Qubole's real traffic come only from AWS.
IAM principal ID: AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS. Any activity from this IAM user should be investigated, because only the attacker used it in the accounts the researchers examined.

Le mercredi 4 novembre, je recevais Arnaud Dubien, chercheur associé à l’IRIS et directeur de l’Observatoire franco-russe, dans mon podcast intitulé « Russie – Ukraine : une guerre sans fin ? ».

À la suite de cette émission, il a fait l’objet d’une vague de critiques injustifiées l’accusant d’être pro-Poutine. Certains en ont aussi profité pour me reprocher de ne pas avoir anticipé l’invasion de l’Ukraine, alors que de nombreux autres spécialistes ne pensaient pas Poutine capable de commettre un tel acte.

Je ne suis pas pro-russe : j’ai, à travers de nombreux livres, énuméré les erreurs stratégiques occidentales, mais aussi celles de Vladimir Poutine, notamment celle de déclencher une guerre contre l’Ukraine. Il est d’ailleurs à noter que ces critiques concernant l’Ukraine me sont adressées avec plus d’entrain depuis mes prises de position sur Gaza.

Ces critiques sont cependant l’occasion d’aborder une question plus large : peut-on réellement prévoir les ruptures stratégiques ? La guerre en Ukraine n’est pas la seule à avoir surpris les analystes. L’invasion du Koweït par l’Irak et les attentats du 11 septembre 2001 ont aussi été des événements inattendus. Quelles leçons en tirer dans l’analyse des relations internationales ?

Face à la surcharge et la manipulation informationnelles, l’enjeu n’est plus, aujourd’hui, seulement de savoir vérifier l’information. Il repose désormais dans le développement de capacités à apprendre de ses erreurs, à questionner ses certitudes et à transformer les perturbations informationnelles en opportunités de progression. Face à ce défi capacitaire de traitement de l’information, trouver de nouveaux outils adaptés apparaît comme une nécessité.

Dans cette optique, Sindup lance Veille Antifragile. Société Coopérative d’Intérêt Collectif spécialisée, Sindup est spécialisée depuis 2004 en veille stratégique et gestion des connaissances. Ce support pédagogique en libre accès invite à apprendre des troubles informationnels pour améliorer ses réflexes et méthodes d’analyse des rapports de force. L’auto-diagnostic, accessible sans création de compte, propose 13 missions regroupant 75 auto-évaluations, suivies de 10 mises en situation.

Après ce parcours d’une quinzaine de minutes, l’utilisateur obtient un indice de maîtrise informationnelle sur 100, une analyse de profil et une représentation de ses résultats sur les 13 dimensions étudiées.

Le bilan met alors en évidence trois points d’appui et trois priorités de progression ainsi que trois idées d’expériences à mener dans les 30 jours pour ancrer de nouvelles habitudes. Pour compléter la démarche, Sindup fournit sur son site un livre blanc “Veille & désinformation à l’ère de l’IA” et des conseils pratiques sur la Veille Antifragile ainsi qu’un podcast issu d’un VeilleLab organisé par le Master VeCIS de l’Université de Lille.

Ainsi, à l’heure où la désinformation est omniprésente, ces outils offrent aux utilisateurs un avantage notable par la connaissance approfondie de leurs biais et des réflexes à mettre en place pour analyser l’information et s’en servir intelligemment ultérieurement.
