title: Trump choisit Stephen Miller. Et donc la guerre.
text:
Trump choisit Stephen Miller. Et donc la guerre.

4 min. de lecture

Citer

Partager

Imprimeren PDF

Ajouter aux favoris

Romuald Sciora

Chercheur associé à l’IRIS, directeur de l’Observatoire politique et géostratégique des États-Unis

Il aura fallu trois jours. Trois petits jours pour que Donald Trump montre ce qu’il avait réellement retenu de la gifle électorale du 3 novembre. Alors que certains commentateurs nous expliquaient déjà, avec leur deni habituel, que le président allait se résigner à son statut de canard boiteux, négocier avec les démocrates et préparer tranquillement sa retraite à Mar-a-Lago, le voilà qui nomme Stephen Miller chef de cabinet de la Maison-Blanche.

Stephen Miller. Pas un républicain modéré. Pas un négociateur. Pas un de ces conservateurs traditionnels qui croient encore aux vertus du compromis. Non. L’un des idéologues les plus radicaux de l’extrême droite américaine, architecte de la politique migratoire de Trump et partisan d’un pouvoir présidentiel toujours plus étendu.

Voilà qui devrait éclairer ceux qui voyaient déjà le président rentrer dans le rang.

Car cette nomination n’a rien d’anodin. Susie Wiles, qui quitte ses fonctions pour rejoindre l’appareil politique trumpiste, avait été chargée de mettre un peu d’ordre dans une Maison-Blanche où le chaos tient souvent lieu de méthode de gouvernement. Miller, lui, n’est pas là pour tempérer les ardeurs présidentielles. Il est là pour les organiser. Et, si possible, les pousser plus loin encore.

Le message est limpide : Trump n’entend pas tirer les conséquences politiques de sa défaite. Il prépare sa contre-attaque.

Il faut dire que le camouflet est considérable. Les démocrates ont repris les deux chambres du Congrès. La guerre en Iran, l’envolée des prix de l’énergie, les droits de douane et les inquiétudes économiques ont fini par coûter cher aux républicains. Une bonne partie de l’Amérique a voulu dire non. Trump, lui, semble avoir décidé de répondre en criant plus fort.

Mais il serait réducteur de n’y voir qu’une nouvelle colère d’un président incapable d’accepter la contradiction.

Le Donald Trump de 2026 n’est plus celui de 2017. À l’époque, il était entouré d’opportunistes et de républicains traditionnels qui espéraient encore pouvoir le tenir en laisse. Aujourd’hui, il dispose d’hommes et de femmes qui savent parfaitement ce qu’ils veulent. Une extrême droite crypto-fasciste, organisée, idéologiquement structurée, dont le projet dépasse largement le sort personnel de celui qui lui a ouvert les portes du pouvoir.

Avec JD Vance à la vice-présidence et Stephen Miller désormais aux commandes de l’appareil présidentiel, cette mouvance consolide son emprise sur la Maison-Blanche. La défaite électorale, loin de la disperser, semble au contraire la pousser à resserrer les rangs.

Ces gens-là n’ont aucune intention d’abandonner un travail déjà bien engagé.

Et c’est précisément ce qui rend les deux années à venir si inquiétantes.

Dès janvier, le nouveau Congrès pourra multiplier les enquêtes, convoquer les responsables de l’administration, examiner les abus de pouvoir et, pourquoi pas, engager une nouvelle procédure de destitution. Les démocrates disposent désormais de moyens institutionnels considérables. Encore faudra-t-il qu’ils sachent s’en servir.

Face à eux, Trump conserve la Maison-Blanche, son droit de veto et un appareil exécutif dont Stephen Miller connaît parfaitement les rouages. Il pourra multiplier les décrets, provoquer les affrontements judiciaires, refuser de coopérer avec certaines commissions parlementaires et transformer chaque tentative de contrôle en nouvelle bataille politique.

Une guerre de tranchées s’annonce entre l’exécutif et le législatif. Et, cette fois, les protagonistes ne semblent même plus s’accorder sur les règles du jeu.

Les affrontements entre le Congrès et la Maison-Blanche ne datent pas d’hier Mais comparer ce qui se prépare aux querelles entre Bill Clinton et Newt Gingrich, ou entre Barack Obama […]

title: Israel’s Foreign Funding Inquiry is Not Evidence of a Stolen Election
text: Voted: A Palestinian citizen of Israel casts her ballot in the country's general election at a polling station in Umm al-Fahm, Israel. Image: Associated Press / Alamy StockThe incumbent appears to be using a national security foreign-funding inquiry to discredit 19 Arab-held seats and perhaps disrupt formation of a replacement government.President Isaac Herzog has entrusted Gadi Eisenkot with forming Israel’s next government after parties holding 67 seats - including the Joint List and Ra’am - recommended him. He has 28 days to turn that support into a government (though this can be extended for up to two weeks).Two days after Israel’s 27 October election, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, who chairs the Central Elections Committee (CEC), wrote to David Zini, the head of Israel’s domestic security service (Shin Bet). He asked for an investigation into ‘serious suspicions’ of ‘improper influence on the elections – exerted through funding provided by foreign entities acting against Israeli interests’, adding that he could not ‘attest to the substance of these suspicions’. Within hours, Likud had a name for the affair, ‘Ra’amgate’, and a verdict: ‘They stole the election in Israel!’.The CEC could not vouch for the suspicions, but – to wide opprobrium – Likud has cast doubt on the election results and on the legitimacy of any government dependent on Arab party support. Investigating foreign campaign money is legitimate; using an unfinished inquiry to discredit the votes of Arab citizens and exclude their representatives from government would, however, be a political manoeuvre.The arithmetic explains the urgency. The final count gave Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc 53 seats and the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot 48, with the Joint List and Ra’am on a combined 19. That is a record for Arab parties, and it is also the difference between either camp and the 61 seats needed for a majority.Likud and other outgoing coalition factions sought to delay certification pending two separate investigations: a Shin Bet inquiry, with Mossad involvement, into suspicions that money from Qatar and other countries reached the Joint List through disguised donations; and a police investigation into alleged vote-buying in the Negev.quoteThe law provides no automatic disqualification for campaign-finance breaches or receipt of foreign funding The CEC nevertheless certified the results on 4 November after reviewing material from 9,069 ballot boxes. It found no irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or altered its outcome. The results were presented to President Isaac Herzog on schedule. In the full committee’s certification vote, 15 representatives voted in favour, two Otzma Yehudit representatives voted against and the other 14 outgoing-coalition representatives abstained. Sohlberg stated that the suspicions remain only suspicions and that ‘even if they are verified, the scope of their potential influence is limited’. He added that they ‘do not cast aspersions on the votes of the Arab community in any way’ and that high turnout is welcome. The login systems behind two car brands' mobile apps could be taken over completely, two security researchers found, allowing them to access any customer's account and, for an owner with a connected car, unlock the doors and start the engine.

Both apps signed customers in through ForgeRock, an identity platform now part of Ping Identity, and on those servers the researchers reached an administrator console that still used its default password.

They tested the full attack only on their own and consenting owners' cars in the United States, in February 2026, and both systems were fixed about two hours after they reported the problem.

Shubham Shah and Sam Curry published their work late last week. They had started with the apps: both brands signed customers in through the same platform, which runs in two parts: one for login and one, called OpenIDM, that holds customer records.

OpenIDM comes with a built-in administrator console powered by the Apache Felix tool. ForgeRock's own hardening guide tells operators to remove this console or protect it before going live because it stores its own password separately from the rest of the system. On these servers, it was still there and still used the documented default: the word admin for both the username and the password.

The console was blocked from the open internet, but the edge that guards the site and the Java software behind it read the same web address differently. By adding encoded slashes and extra characters, the researchers made the edge treat the request as a harmless static file while the server treated it as the path to the console, and the default password did the rest. The full method is in their technical analysis.

Inside the console, the researchers used a built-in scheduler to run small scripts that execute their own code on the identity server. That gave them a command prompt on the machine that holds the customer records for both brands' logins.

The records sat behind the same block as the console, but the researchers' code reached them from inside the server. They changed a target account's email address and password, signed in as that customer through the normal app, and received the same access tokens the real app uses.

Those tokens were the keys to the car. Using the account's own vehicle commands, the researchers unlocked the doors and started the engine of a test car, with the owner standing next to it, then stopped the engine and locked it again.

The researchers were careful about what they had shown. They reported being able to open a session for any customer account on the affected servers, but they ran the vehicle commands only on cars they owned or were allowed to use. They said they "tested the complete chain only with US accounts and vehicles."

Shubham Shah published a second attack on the Australian systems behind the same brands. There, the way in was different: admin credentials for the identity server had been left in the app's code, intended for a test setup. He set out the full Australia chain in a separate post.

With both attacks together, the researchers said, they could send unlock and engine-start commands to the brands' cars in Australia, the United States, and Canada. That second post does not give a date for when the Australian systems were fixed.

The attack left little for an owner to notice. Changing the email and password did not log the owner out of their app, and the researchers could direct the account's alerts to their own phone, keeping them off the owner's phone.

Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That’s the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets, including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories.
The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local “.claude/settings.local.json” file on the user’s computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it.
This isn’t really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user’s local machine (assuming that machine doesn’t become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer’s global .gitignore list, which usually prevents it from being shared publicly.
But that .gitignore setting isn’t reflected at the repo level, meaning the sensitive file can be uploaded accidentally if a repo is cloned to another machine or a folder becomes a repo later, for instance. In many cases, Claude Code itself will commit changes to the settings file without the user’s input, Apiiro writes.

Apiiro’s researchers found over 100,000 cases where Claude Code’s local settings file had been uploaded to a public GitHub repository. Of these, only about 1,100 from 63 different organizations contained secrets such as public API tokens, database passwords, or private keys. Even after these files are discovered and removed from a repository, the secrets can persist in forks of the original project if a GitHub user isn’t careful.

What’s to be done?
Although this security issue is getting more attention now, it was flagged in a Claude Code bug report as far back as August 2025. Other bug reports also noted that the sensitive settings file was sometimes not added to the user’s .gitignore list or that Claude Code could add the sensitive commands to another file that was not protected from git sharing. These bug reports were all closed without action after 60 days of inactivity.
In a comment thread on Hacker News over the weekend, Claude Code’s Boris Cherny said the team is “looking into what we can do to prevent this.” That said, he noted that these settings files should pretty much never be checked in to a user’s git source control and that cases like these seemed to come up only when “the files were manually created and checked in.”
In the meantime, Cherny recommended using Claude Code’s auto mode, which uses classifiers to automatically route “routine permission prompts” without requiring what Cherny calls “manually maintaining finicky allow/deny lists.” But when another user noted that sensitive commands can still be saved to settings files in auto mode, Cherny said that was a “good catch” and added that the team is “thinking through what we can do to improve this.”
Cherny also recommends Claude Code users make use of secret scanners—which can trawl files for sensitive information and scrub it out—and said that the team was considering building this kind of secret scanning into Claude Code itself in the future. That said, the Apiiro researchers found that 215 of the roughly 1,100 public secrets it found in Claude Code settings files were not flagged by two popular secret scanners, gitleaks and TruffleHog.

November 9, 2026 By Amar Ćemanović — Leave a Comment XLinkedInRedditFacebook

York University has disclosed a cybersecurity incident in which an unauthorized actor stole personal information from departmental online forms.

The university discovered the incident on October 25, 2026, and brought in external experts to investigate and help secure the affected systems. It has not disclosed how many people were affected, how the attacker gained access, or when the unauthorized access began.

York is a Toronto-based teaching and research university with more than 53,500 students enrolled across over 200 undergraduate and graduate degree programs, and a global alumni network of approximately 390,000 people.

According to its incident notice, the theft involves information submitted through forms used for meeting registrations, residence applications, surveys, and other university business. The affected submission periods vary by department, with the earliest stretching from 2007 through October 2026.

Sensitive information among stolen records

York identified affected forms on 14 departmental and faculty websites, including the Department of Psychology, Division of Students, Faculty of Graduate Studies, Faculty of Science, Lassonde School of Engineering, and Schulich School of Business. Housing services, the Centre for Refugee Studies, and other administrative and research units were also affected.

The oldest affected submissions came from the Faculty of Environmental and Urban Change, dating to 2007. Other departments’ affected records date from 2013 to 2022.

Depending on the individual and form, stolen information includes contact details, dates of birth, York identification numbers, academic and employment histories, photographs, and family or third-party contact information.

More sensitive categories include diagnoses and treatment information, disability and accommodation status, income and debts, citizenship or origin, race and ethnicity, Indigenous status, religion, sexual orientation, vaccination status, and legal or criminal background information.

York emphasized that the categories listed for each department do not apply to every affected person. Most stolen information consisted of university identification numbers and contact details.

Notifications and credit monitoring

York says its investigation found no evidence that the attacker accessed other parts of its IT environment. The university has implemented security improvements to its web forms and reported the incident to law enforcement and Ontario’s Information and Privacy Commissioner.

For people covered by the listed groups and submission periods, the public notice serves as notification. York will directly email a smaller group, including individuals whose government identification or financial account information was exposed, offering eligible recipients two years of free TransUnion credit monitoring and identity theft protection.

Affected individuals can contact incident@yorku.ca to learn what information was stolen, subject to identity verification. York warns that responses may take time.

The university advises watching for suspicious emails, texts, and calls, monitoring financial accounts, and using unique passwords and multifactor authentication.

Google DeepMind says AI agents working under human supervision have found two ways to reduce the cost of attacking 1024-bit RSA cryptosystems.

The research, conducted with cryptographers from UC San Diego and Inria, indicates that attacks on legacy RSA-1024 require less computation than previously assumed.

“In practice, these results only affect obsolete 1024-bit RSA systems, and modern encryption protocols, which almost universally use 2048-bit or larger keys, remain secure,” said Pushmeet Kohli, VP at Google DeepMind and chief scientist at Google Cloud.

The first finding involves digital signatures and padding, the preset data that many signature standards add to a message to bring it to a fixed block size. Padding was known to make forgery harder, but its value against an attacker who can choose what gets signed was unclear.

DeepMind determined that it depends on the share of the signed block the attacker controls. “Once they control roughly half of the block or more, padding adds no protection at all,” Kohli explained.

According to the accompanying paper, this applies to the PKCS#1 v1.5 format used by the PKCS#11 signing interface of cryptographic devices such as hardware security modules (HSMs).

In a sandboxed test, the agents re-ran an earlier academic forgery attack on the same 1024-bit key, cutting CPU time 3.5-fold. The first forgery took 391 CPU core-years, versus 1,380 in the original study.

Two AI agents designed, ran and debugged the forgery computation in under four days, with approximately 20 messages from the human researcher, mostly approvals. The key was not factored; that would take an estimated 500,000 to 1 million core-years.

Forgery is harder when the attacker controls less of the block, such as a 32-byte hash. Even then, DeepMind found an algorithm that by its theoretical estimates is roughly 1,600 times better than the previous best method against 1024-bit keys.

The second finding concerns factoring many RSA keys of the same size, where an attacker can share the cost of one large upfront computation across all of them.

DeepMind’s agents came up with an algorithm that makes factoring each additional 1024-bit key roughly 30 times cheaper on average than the best previous approach. However, this theoretical estimate assumes an initial computation as costly as factoring one key, and the method has not been implemented.

The researchers noted that the signature attack does not recover the private key. It requires roughly 4 billion signing queries made in advance, and does not work against devices that hash messages internally.

“Together, these results show that in a new era of AI-enabled mathematics and computation, we cannot treat cryptographic hardness as a fixed assumption. Using AI to rigorously test our previously held assumptions will ensure that modern encryption stays secure,” Kohli said.

U.S. government agencies have warned that threat actors are actively targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems globally with an aim to cause service disruptions, fire hazards, and loss of inventory.

"The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards," according to a joint advisory.

According to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), Department of Agriculture (USDA), and Department of Transportation (DOT), threat actors are likely to exploit authentication bypasses, arbitrary code injection, and weak configurations to gain access to these systems and cause the following effects -

Change of temperature, which, in turn, could affect the service life of the system, create a fire hazard, cause inventory loss, or harm consumers who purchase products after unsafe storage.
Loss of visibility into current temperatures due to a denial-of-service.

In response to the threat, owners and operators are being urged to use strong authentication, keep systems updated, identify any systems that are accessible from the internet, isolate operational technology (OT) devices, change default passwords, retire and replace legacy devices, remove unnecessary remote access, and secure necessary remote access.

"Industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems protect food, medicine, and other temperature-sensitive products, making them attractive targets for malicious cyber actors," said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman.

"We are seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk."

In recent weeks, threat actors have targeted hundreds of supermarkets across Europe by exploiting weaknesses in internet-accessible refrigeration controllers to raise temperatures, in some cases to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit), or force cooling units into defrost mode, spoiling food and resulting in financial losses.

Targets of these attacks ranged from major supermarket chains to small grocers and butchers in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Sweden, and the U.K.

Among those targeted was the French Blood Establishment, which confirmed that a cybersecurity incident affecting a refrigeration equipment provider had raised temperature and defrost settings to "extremely high levels" at three facilities used to store blood plasma. It's unclear who is behind the hacking spree.

Data from Censys shows that there are still hundreds of Danfoss StoreView instances exposed globally, with most of them located in France, although the number has dropped significantly from 3,004 to 708 between October 9 and November 5, 2026. The Copeland/Dixell XWEB exposure, likewise, has declined from 3,708 to 2,420.

The attack surface management platform described the refrigeration attacks across Europe as the latest addition to a list of other recent incidents targeting critical infrastructure, including gas station tank gauges, air raid systems, and water towers.

"North America accounts for roughly 38% of global ICS [industrial control systems] exposure," Censys said. "Asia's share grew from 22% in 2024 to 25% in 2026, while Europe's fell from 36.5% to 32%. However, these shifts have not produced an overall decline."

Who Gives A Crap, the Australian toilet paper company known for its recycled products and irreverent branding, has revealed that hackers accessed its customer information via an external marketing software provider.
The breach spans customers in Australia, the UK, and the US. Canadian customers have reportedly not been affected.
The company has yet to confirm how many customers were affected.
According to ABC News, an unauthorized party accessed names, phone numbers, mailing and email addresses, as well as information about how much each customer had spent with the company.
